issues.legal_issue: Applicants whose allotment was delayed by an administrative change should not be charged a higher premium than the rate applicable to the sites for which they originally applied when they did not cause the delay and no additional development cost was shown.
material_facts: The applicants had applied for larger sites and were selected in an initial draw, but the administration changed the allotment plan before issuing allotment letters.
The applicants did not cause the delay and had not applied for the smaller sites in the later plan.
Entrepreneurs allotted sites under the original plan paid the lower premium rate.
There was no evidence that the administration incurred greater expenditure in forming the later sites.
issues.conclusion: The direction that the applicants be charged the original, lower premium rate was justified.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the circumstances of the allotment: the applicants had sought the sites offered under the original plan, the administration's policy change caused the delay, and no additional expenditure justified charging them more than comparable allottees. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: administration_appeals_reduced_premium and applicants_did_not_cause_delay and administrative_change_caused_delay and no_evidence_of_added_development_cost and comparable_original_allottees_paid_lower_rate

predicates.administration_appeals_reduced_premium: The administration challenges a direction reducing the premium payable by applicants for sites.
predicates.applicants_did_not_cause_delay: The applicants did not cause the delay in completing their allotment.
predicates.administrative_change_caused_delay: The administration changed its allotment plan, causing the delay.
predicates.no_evidence_of_added_development_cost: No evidence shows that forming the later sites cost more than forming the originally proposed sites.
predicates.comparable_original_allottees_paid_lower: Other allottees under the original plan paid a lower premium rate than the rate later demanded from the applicants.

issues.definition: When the administration appeals a reduced premium, and the applicants did not cause the administration's delay, no added development cost is shown, and comparable original allottees paid less, the applicants pay the original premium rate.

issues.legal_issue: Selection in a preliminary draw does not create a right to obtain a site without official communication of the allotment.
material_facts: The applicants were selected in a preliminary draw for larger sites.
The administration did not issue allotment letters or otherwise officially communicate an allotment to them.
The applicants claimed a right to take possession based on the draw.
issues.conclusion: The applicants had no right to obtain transfer of the sites because no official allotment communication had been issued.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 8(3) of the Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973, the allotment must be communicated by registered post with particulars of the site and premium. The Court held that such intimation confers the right to obtain possession. No earlier case was cited for this point.

predicates.appeal_claims_site_transfer_from_prelimi: An appeal claims a right to obtain a site based on selection in a preliminary draw.
predicates.no_official_allotment_communication: The administration did not officially communicate the allotment and its particulars to the applicant.

issues.definition: If an appeal claims a site based on a preliminary draw but the administration did not officially communicate the allotment, there is no right to obtain the site.

issues.legal_issue: The requirement that an administrator allot a site after receiving an application and deposit gives an applicant a right to consideration, not an automatic right to allotment.
material_facts: The applicants submitted applications with the required earnest money.
There were more applicants than available sites, and the administration used a draw to select applicants.
The applicants argued that the rule's use of the word “shall” required the administrator to allot them sites.
issues.conclusion: The applicants were entitled only to have their applications considered; submission and acceptance of an application did not create a right to a site.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 8(3) of the Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973, was read in context and in light of the rule's purpose. The Court held that treating “shall” as mandatory would require allotment to every applicant and defeat a workable process for considering competing applications. The meaning of “shall” depends on context, purpose, and the consequences of the competing interpretations.

rule.if: appeal_claims_automatic_site_allotment and application_submitted_with_earnest_money and applications_exceeded_available_sites and allotment_requires_comparison_of_applicants

predicates.appeal_claims_automatic_site_allotment: An appeal asserts that submitting an application requires the administrator to allot a site automatically.
predicates.application_submitted_with_earnest_money: An applicant submitted an application accompanied by the required earnest money.
predicates.applications_exceeded_available_sites: The number of applicants exceeded the number of sites available.
predicates.allotment_requires_comparison_of_applica: The administrator must consider competing applications and select among applicants when sites are insufficient.

issues.definition: If an applicant seeks automatic allotment after applying with earnest money, but applicants outnumber sites and selection requires comparison, the application gives a right to consideration rather than a site.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot compel a public authority to carry out an assurance that conflicts with binding legal procedure or exceeds the authority's power.
material_facts: The applicants relied on the administration's demand for an additional payment and the preliminary draw as assurances that they would receive the larger sites.
No specific assurance promising those particular sites was established.
The claimed assurance would have required the administration to allot particular sites without following the governing allotment procedure.
issues.conclusion: Promissory estoppel could not require the administration to allot the sites; the applicants had established no specific assurance, and even an assurance contrary to the governing rules could not be enforced.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule that promissory estoppel is reliance-based and does not require proof of separate detriment, while holding that it cannot be used to compel a public body to perform a promise contrary to law or beyond its authority. It relied on Delhi Cloth & General Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Civil Appeal No. 223 of 1974, disposed of on October 8, 1987.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_in_public_allo: An applicant invokes promissory estoppel to require a public authority to allot a particular site.
predicates.no_specific_assurance_of_particular_site: The public authority did not specifically assure the applicant that a particular site would be allotted.
predicates.requested_promise_conflicts_with_binding: The requested performance would require the public authority to act contrary to the governing procedure or beyond its authority.

issues.definition: When an applicant invokes promissory estoppel to compel a public authority to allot a particular site, the authority cannot be compelled if it made no specific assurance or the requested allotment conflicts with binding procedure.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority may revise a site-allotment plan when the original area lacks enough sites and the revised layout is adopted bona fide to address that shortage.
material_facts: The administration concluded that the original area did not have enough sites to accommodate the applicants.
It formed a layout of smaller sites in another area to accommodate more applicants.
The Court found no material showing that enough sites existed under the original plan and found no reason to doubt the bona fides of the administrative action.
issues.conclusion: The administration's decision to replace the original plan with a layout of smaller sites was not improper on the evidence before the Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that revising the plan would not be proper if enough sites existed under the original plan to accommodate the applicants. In the absence of material establishing that circumstance, and where the administration acted bona fide to address the shortage, the revision was upheld.

rule.if: challenge_to_revised_site_plan and original_area_lacked_enough_sites and revised_layout_addressed_shortage and administrative_action_was_bona_fide

predicates.challenge_to_revised_site_plan: A proceeding challenges an administrative decision to replace an original site-allotment plan with a revised plan.
predicates.original_area_lacked_enough_sites: The original area did not contain enough sites to accommodate the applicants.
predicates.revised_layout_addressed_shortage: The administration formed a revised layout to address the shortage of sites under the original plan.
predicates.administrative_action_was_bona_fide: The administration adopted the revised layout bona fide rather than for an improper purpose.

issues.definition: When a revised site plan is challenged, the original area lacks enough sites, and a bona fide revised layout addresses that shortage, the revised plan is permissible.

issues.legal_issue: Grouping applicants seeking sites for the same kind of activity and considering them together for smaller sites is not discriminatory when the original area lacks sufficient sites and the revised arrangement is rationally related to accommodating applicants.
material_facts: All applicants sought industrial sites for establishing printing presses and were considered together.
The original area lacked enough sites to accommodate them.
The administration formed a second layout of smaller sites, and the applicants were considered for sites under that plan.
The Court found no arbitrariness in the grouping or in considering the applicants for smaller sites.
issues.conclusion: The revised policy was not arbitrary or discriminatory and did not violate the guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution prohibits class legislation but permits reasonable classification based on an intelligible differentia with a rational relation to the objective pursued; exact equality is not required, and arbitrary State action is prohibited. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, [1959] SCR 279; Re The Special Courts Bill, 1978, [1979] 2 SCR 476; E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, [1974] 2 SCR 348; and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, AIR 1978 SC 597.

rule.if: challenge_alleges_discrimination_in_site_allotment and applicants_share_relevant_activity and applicants_considered_together and original_area_lacked_enough_sites and revised_grouping_had_rational_connection_to_accommodating_applicants

predicates.challenge_alleges_discrimination_in_site: A proceeding alleges that a revised site-allotment policy discriminates against applicants.
predicates.applicants_share_relevant_activity: The applicants sought sites for the same kind of activity.
predicates.applicants_considered_together: The administration grouped and considered the applicants together.
predicates.original_area_lacked_enough_sites: The original area did not contain enough sites to accommodate the applicants.
predicates.revised_grouping_had_rational_connection: The administration's grouping and revised site arrangement were rationally connected to accommodating applicants despite the shortage.

issues.definition: When applicants seeking sites for the same activity are considered together, the original area is insufficient, and the revised arrangement rationally addresses that shortage, the policy is not arbitrary or discriminatory.
